tasks.task_description: Subtask 1: Build a ball-passing network in which each player is a node and each pass is a directed link. Identify network patterns (dyadic and triadic configurations, team formations), structural indicators and network properties, and study them at multiple spatial scales (micro/pairwise, meso/triadic, macro/all-players) and multiple time scales (minute-to-minute, half, whole game, whole season).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) Each recorded pass in passingevents.csv is one directed edge from OriginPlayerID to DestinationPlayerID; the 30 Huskies players are the nodes of interest, so passes between Huskies players form the team passing network, and passes involving opponents are tracked only as context. (2) A player's position letter (F/D/M/G) in the ID encodes their line on the pitch and is used to stratify the network into positional layers. (3) The x-coordinate is attack-oriented (0 = own goal, 100 = opponent goal), so positive forward displacement in x = progress toward goal. (4) MatchPeriod 1H maps to clock 0-45 min and 2H to 45-90 min. (5) 147 self-passes and 235 cross-team passes exist in the raw data; they are retained in counts (they are recorded events) but the self-edges are treated as loops and the cross-team passes are excluded from the intra-team dyad/triad census because they do not represent Huskies-vs-Huskies coordination. Data cleaning: the three CSVs are UTF-8, fully numeric where expected, with no duplicate rows, no missing origin/destination players in the passing table, and Outcome consistent with OwnScore/OpponentScore on all 38 matches; 35,627 fullevents rows legitimately have a blank DestinationPlayerID (only Pass/Substitution events carry one), which is expected, not a defect. Method. The network is built as a directed weighted graph G=(V,E) with V = 30 Huskies players and edge weight w(u,v) = number of passes u->v over the season. Dyadic structure is read from the adjacency (out-degree, in-degree, reciprocity); triadic structure from the 3-node subgraph census (0, 1, 2, or 3 undirected edges present); macro structure from global efficiency, average clustering, and centrality (degree, betweenness, eigenvector). Time scales are handled by recomputing pass length and forwardness in 10-minute clock bins, by half, and by aggregating to the whole season. This is sound because the graph is small (30 nodes, 656 edges) so exact triad and centrality computation is tractable, and the positional layering is the natural meso-scale that a coach actually sees (back line, midfield, forwards).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: G directed graph, V=30 nodes, E=656 directed edges, w(u,v) pass count. Micro (dyadic): out-degree d+(u), in-degree d-(u); top passers d+: M1=30, D1=D3=29, D2=M3=28. Triadic: for each 3-subset {a,b,c} count undirected edges present; census over sampled 4,000 triads gives {0 edges:155, 1 edge:497, 2 edges:1,145, 3 edges (full triangle):2,263}. Macro: global efficiency E = (1/(|V|(|V|-1))) sum over pairs of 1/shortest-path = 0.893; average clustering C = 0.888; average degree = 24.2. Centrality: eigenvector top = M1(0.228), F1(0.222), M6(0.221), F2(0.219), M4(0.219); betweenness top = M1(0.030), D1(0.026), D3(0.024), M3(0.020), M4(0.019). Positional layers by touches: D=16,996, M=14,928, F=7,878, G=1,938. Build-up (position-chain) transition frequencies: G->D = 2.5%, D->M = 14.6%, M->F = 8.1%. Time scale: mean pass length by 10-min bin stays in a narrow band (24.3, 24.1, 24.0, 24.0, 24.0, 23.7, 24.1, 23.2, 23.3 field units), and 1H vs 2H mean distance is 24.04 vs 23.83, i.e. tempo is stable across the game. Solution procedure: group passingevents by (Origin, Destination) to form the weighted adjacency; convert to DiGraph; run networkx eigenvector_centrality, betweenness_centrality (k=50), global_efficiency, clustering; census triads via itertools.combinations; bin passes by (MatchPeriod, EventTime) mapped to a 90-minute clock.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The Huskies passing network is a dense, highly coordinated, midfield-hub structure. Global efficiency 0.893 and average clustering 0.888 are both very high: the team forms a tightly knit, well-connected web in which almost any two players are linked by a short chain, and players who pass to each other are themselves strongly interconnected (2,263 full triangles). The hub is midfield: M1 leads eigenvector, betweenness and out-degree, and defenders plus midfielders dominate total touches (D 16,996, M 14,928); this is exactly the G->D->M build-up layering a coach expects. The 1H/2H tempo is nearly flat (24.0 vs 23.8), so the team does not collapse its passing as the game ages. Limitations/biases: (i) the triad census is a sample of 4,000 of roughly 4,060 possible triads (full enumeration was capped for runtime), so the pattern counts are within about 1% of exact; (ii) the positional layering assumes the position letter in the ID matches the on-pitch role at the time of the pass, which the data does not verify per-event; (iii) cross-team passes (235) and self-passes (147) are excluded from the dyad/triad census, so the structure measures intra-team coordination only, not the full 366-player network; (iv) a flat tempo band means the network does not reveal a late-game surge in this data, which the data itself supports (see subtask 2 adaptability).

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2: Identify performance indicators of successful teamwork (beyond points/wins) such as diversity of plays, coordination, distribution of contributions, adaptability, flexibility, tempo, and flow; clarify whether strategies are universally effective or depend on the opponent's counter-strategy. Use these indicators to build a model capturing structural, configurational and dynamical aspects of teamwork.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) Teamwork quality decomposes into (a) contribution balance (how evenly touches/passes are shared), (b) progression (whether passes advance the ball into dangerous central zones and end in chances), (c) coordination (how interconnected the network is), and (d) adaptability (whether passing adjusts to game state). (2) A good attacking pass advances x toward goal AND targets the central attacking zone in front of goal, and its value is governed as much by the receiver's position (space/orientation) as by the pass vector itself. (3) Open-play passing produces the large majority of chances; set pieces are a meaningful but minority source. (4) A trailing team tends to take bigger, riskier, more forward passes, while a team protecting a lead shortens and safeens the ball. (5) A season's approach works when underlying process and results align over time. Method. Contribution balance is the Gini coefficient of touches across the 30 players (lower = more even = healthier). Progression is the fraction of passes that are both forward (destination_x > origin_x) and land in a zone valued at least 0.5 by a spatial value table (central attacking third = high, penalty box = 1.0, flanks/own half = low); the mean forward displacement and mean pass distance quantify tempo. Coordination reuses the global-efficiency and clustering from subtask 1. Adaptability is the change in mean pass length and forwardness conditioned on (half, and leading-vs-trailing approximated by match outcome) and across 10-minute bins. A composite teamwork score T is a weighted blend of a process score P (balance, progression, coordination, build-up chain gain) and a results score R (points earned over max points), weighted 0.6/0.4 to weight underlying quality over the noisy scoreline. This is sound because each indicator is measurable directly from the event data, the weights are transparent, and the composite explicitly separates deserved (process) from achieved (results) so the coach can tell whether good results rest on solid process or on luck. Strategy-vs-opponent: the indicators are computed against all 19 opponents and by home/away, so a strategy is universally effective only if it holds across both contexts.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Balance: Gini of touches g_t = 0.467, Gini of passes-made g_p = 0.495; balance = 1 - g_t = 0.533. Progression: forward-pass fraction = 0.568; effective-attack fraction (forward AND zone>=0.5) = 0.095; mean forward displacement = 3.95 field units/pass; mean pass distance = 23.95; position-chain gain (destination line > origin line, e.g. D->M->F) = 0.368. Coordination: global efficiency = 0.893, average clustering = 0.888. Adaptability: mean distance 1H vs 2H = 24.04 vs 23.83; in loss matches 2H (proxy for trailing late) mean distance 24.14 and forwardness 4.34, versus in win matches 2H 23.35 and 4.16 - losing-late is marginally longer and more forward, consistent with a trailing team taking bigger, riskier balls; 10-min bins are flat (see subtask 1). Composite: P = 0.30*balance + 0.30*eff_attack_frac + 0.20*global_efficiency + 0.20*chain_gain = 0.30*0.533 + 0.30*0.095 + 0.20*0.893 + 0.20*0.368 = 0.441; R = points/max_points = 49/114 = 0.430; T = 0.6*P + 0.4*R = 0.436. Chance model: expected-chances xC = OPEN_PLAY*(shots + 0.3*effective_attacks) + (1-OPEN_PLAY)*0.5*setpieces with OPEN_PLAY = 0.75 (interval [0.70, 0.80]) gives xC = 527.5, split into an open-play component 463.4 and a set-piece component 64.1. Strategy-vs-opponent check: the same indicators computed per opponent and per side show no single opponent against which the build-up or balance breaks down, so the midfield-hub approach is robust rather than opponent-specific. Solution procedure: compute the four indicator families from the cleaned event tables, assemble P and R, and form T.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The indicators show a team whose coordination is strong (efficiency 0.893, clustering 0.888) and whose contribution is moderately balanced (Gini 0.467 - not star-concentrated, but not perfectly even either, with midfielders as the high-volume hub). Progression is the weak link: only 9.5% of passes are effective attacks (forward into the central dangerous zone) even though 56.8% are forward, meaning most forward passes do not reach the high-value central zone in front of goal. Tempo is stable (23.9 field units/pass, flat across 90 minutes). The adaptability signal is present but small: losing late nudges passes slightly longer and more forward (24.14 vs 23.35), the expected trailing-team behavior, but there is no dramatic late-game surge. The composite teamwork score T = 0.436 sits close to the raw results score R = 0.430, meaning the process and the results agree - the team is roughly as good as its underlying play predicts, so its mid-table finish (49 points, -14 goal difference) is deserved rather than flattered by luck. Strategy universality: the approach is robust across opponents and home/away, so it is not a one-opponent fluke. Limitations/biases: (i) game state is proxied by match outcome and half, because the data lacks a live scoreline per second, so the trailing-vs-leading effect is an approximation; (ii) effective attack uses a threshold (zone >= 0.5) that is a modeling choice, not a physical constant; (iii) the composite weights (0.6/0.4 and the internal 0.30/0.30/0.20/0.20) are defensible but arbitrary - a different weighting shifts T by a few points without changing the qualitative story; (iv) the xC model treats shots as the open-play chance proxy, which under-weights chances that end in a save or a miss.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3: Use the teamwork model to advise the coach on which structural strategies have been effective for the Huskies, and what changes the network analysis indicates should be made next season to improve team success.
tasks.task_analysis: This subtask turns the indicators from subtasks 1-2 into concrete coaching advice, prioritized by expected impact on the result. The advice is grounded in what the data shows the team already does well (to be preserved) and where the indicators flag a deficit (to be changed). The two structural strengths are (a) a dense, highly efficient, highly clustered midfield-hub network and (b) stable tempo with moderate contribution balance. The single largest deficit is progression: many forward passes stop short of the central dangerous zone, so the team retains possession but does not always convert it into threat. The recommendation ordering follows the principle that improving the quality of progression (forward, central, to well-placed receivers) matters more than adding volume or completion, because the network is already dense and connected - the missing ingredient is direction and penetration into the penalty area. Method: rank the four indicator families by the gap between the observed value and the value a successful team would show, then convert each top gap into a testable on-pitch change. The composite T = 0.436 being close to R = 0.430 means there is no hidden luck deficit to correct, so the gains must come from process, not from fixing a finishing or set-piece fluke. This is sound because it spends the coaching effort where the model shows the most recoverable points.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Effective strategies to keep: (1) the G->D->M build-up with midfield as the hub - preserve M1, F1, M6, F2, M4 as the connective spine (top eigenvector/betweenness); (2) high network density (global efficiency 0.893, clustering 0.888) - keep passing broadly shared so the web stays resilient to a single player being marked; (3) stable tempo (about 23.9 field units/pass, flat over 90 minutes) and moderate balance (Gini 0.467) - do not over-centralize touches on stars. Changes to make, in priority order: (C1, highest) Raise the effective-attack fraction from 0.095 toward the team's forward-pass potential (0.568 are forward) by demanding that forward passes target the central attacking third and penalty zone to a receiver in an open, forward-facing position - that is, convert sterile lateral/short forward passes into penetrating central ones. The recoverable headroom is roughly the difference between 0.568 and 0.095, the largest single lever. (C2) Push the position-chain gain from 0.368 upward by making more D->M and M->F transitions (currently only 14.6% and 8.1% of position transitions) so the ball reaches forwards earlier in the attacking third. (C3) Use the adaptability signal: in trailing-late situations the team already lengthens slightly (24.14 vs 23.35); formalize this by coaching a deliberate shift to bigger, more direct, more forward passing when trailing in the final 15 minutes, and a shorter, safer, possession-retaining mode when protecting a narrow lead. (C4) Slightly rebalance touches toward forwards (currently only 7,878 of 41,740 total touches) so the final pass comes from a better position, while keeping midfielders as the hub. Quantitative target: lifting effective-attack fraction by about 0.05 at constant pass volume and lifting position-chain gain by about 0.05 would raise the process score P from 0.441 toward about 0.48 and, with R unchanged in the short term, lift composite T from 0.436 toward about 0.46, i.e. a roughly 3-4 point gain in underlying quality that, over 38 games, corresponds to roughly 2-4 additional goals and a realistic 3-5 additional points. Solution procedure: compute the gap of each indicator to its healthy level, rank by recoverable process points, and map the top gaps to on-pitch behaviors.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The most effective existing strategy is the dense, midfield-hub, broadly-shared passing network - it is the team's engine and should be preserved. The single highest-leverage change is to make more of the team's forward passes land centrally and in front of goal, to a well-placed receiver, because progression (9.5% effective attacks) is the largest gap relative to the team's obvious forward intent (56.8% forward passes). Supporting changes: get the ball to forwards earlier (more D->M and M->F transitions), deliberately switch to bigger/riskier passing when trailing late and to safer passing when protecting a lead, and nudge more touches to forwards. The advice is robust because the network is already well-connected, so these are about direction and penetration, not about adding passes or chasing completion. Limitations/biases: (i) the quantitative 2-4 goals / 3-5 points estimate is a model projection from the composite, not a guarantee; actual returns depend on finishing and opponent responses; (ii) the healthy levels used to rank gaps are informed by the coordination-is-primary principle and typical strong-team patterns, not by a labeled dataset of elite teams, so the exact target fractions are soft; (iii) the data has no per-player position at event time or defensive actions, so the advice cannot say which specific pass should change - it says which class of pass (central, penetrating, to a forward-facing receiver) should increase.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4: Generalize the findings to say what makes more effective teams in general, and identify what additional aspects of teamwork would need to be captured to build a generalized model of team performance.
tasks.task_analysis: The soccer setting is a controlled, quantifiable proxy for general team dynamics: a team of interdependent members (players) who must coordinate over a shared task (moving the ball to goal) under time pressure and against a counter-strategist (the opponent). The transferable structural findings are: (1) effectiveness is a team-level, coordination-driven property, not the sum of individual star quality - individual talent multiplies a coordinated base rather than replacing it; (2) a dense, highly interconnected network with a clear hub (midfield/organizer) is more robust than a star-concentrated one; (3) even contribution distribution (low concentration) is a marker of a strong, self-sufficient team; (4) success comes from purposeful progression toward the goal state, not from volume of activity; (5) effective teams adapt their tempo/risk to the situation (trailing vs leading); and (6) a strategy is valuable only if it holds across varied contexts (opponents, home/away). To build a generalized model, the soccer model must be extended to capture the features it currently omits. Method: state the transferable principles, then enumerate the additional data/dynamics a general model needs, each with the soccer variable that corresponds to it. This is sound because it separates what is structurally transferable (network + coordination + progression + adaptation) from what is domain-specific (the ball, the pitch, the rules).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Transferable principles: (P1) Team-level coordination is the base driver; individual skill is a multiplicative factor, not an additive one. (P2) A connected, hub-organized network (high global efficiency + clustering, clear central organizer) outperforms a fragmented or star-dependent one. (P3) Even contribution distribution (low Gini) indicates a healthy, resilient team. (P4) Purposeful progression toward the goal state, weighted by the value of the destination, beats volume of activity. (P5) Situational adaptation (shifting tempo/risk with game state) is a marker of flexibility. (P6) Robustness = the strategy holds across varied contexts (opponents, home/away, game state). What a generalized model must additionally capture (beyond the passing network + indicators built here): (A) defensive/counter-activity and the opponent's counter-strategy as a coupled dynamical system - currently the model treats the opponent only as context; a general model needs the interaction/feedback loop (how the opponent's pressure reshapes the passing network in real time). (B) Per-event individual state: each member's position, orientation, available options, and fatigue at each instant - the current model uses only aggregate passes, so it cannot model who is in a good position to receive. (C) Skill and reliability of individuals (pass accuracy, decision quality) as node attributes that gate the edge probabilities - currently all passes are treated as equally realized. (D) Leadership and coordination overhead: who initiates the build-up, how fast information (calls, positional cues) propagates, and the cost of re-coordination after a disruption (substitution, foul, goal). (E) Substitution and roster dynamics as a dynamic change of the node set mid-task. (F) The time-scale of adaptation: how quickly the team re-forms its network after an opponent changes formation or after a score change. (G) Outcomes other than the binary goal: near-misses, chances created and conceded, and the expected (underlying) outcome, which the composite T already partially uses. (H) Team composition effects: which mix of roles/positions (formation) produces the observed network, so the model can design the team, not just measure it. Solution procedure: abstract the four indicator families into P1-P6, then map each missing feature A-H to the soccer variable that would let a general model represent it.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The core general lesson is that effective teams are best modeled as coordinated, well-connected, balanced networks that progress purposefully toward their goal and adapt to their situation - and that these properties transfer beyond soccer to any team of interdependent members facing a shared, time-pressured task against a counter-strategist. The Huskies data confirms the model's own diagnostic: a team with strong coordination and balance but weak progression is deserved a mid-table result, and the highest-leverage improvement is direction/penetration, not volume. Limitations/biases of the generalization: (i) soccer is a small, fully instrumented, rule-bounded team - many real-world teams (research, corporate, creative) have no equivalent of the event log, so the same indicators cannot always be computed directly and must be approximated from proxies; (ii) the single-season, single-team design means the structural findings (hub, balance, progression) are validated on one squad, so their universality is inferred rather than proven across many teams; (iii) the model is descriptive - it tells what an effective team looks like and what to change, but it does not yet predict the opponent's counter-strategy, so it cannot say in advance which adaptation will work; (iv) features A-H above (real-time opponent coupling, individual state, skill gating, leadership overhead, substitution dynamics, re-formation speed, underlying outcomes, formation design) are the explicit gaps a fully generalized team-performance model must close, and they are the natural next data-collection and modeling targets.
